You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

# i3-style

Make your i3 config a little more stylish.

About

i3-style applies a theme to your i3 config file to change the colorscheme of window decorations and the different parts of i3bar. It is designed especially for people who frequently change colorschemes.

- Easy to try out new themes.
- Themes are easy to read, modify, and share.
- Modifies your theme in place; templates are not required.

Usage

Call the tool with the name of the theme (or a path to a theme file) and the output location. The tool will apply the theme to your i3 configuration.

Example:

    i3-style solarized -o ~/.config/i3/config --reload

Or apply a theme file directly:

    i3-style ~/.config/i3/solarized.yaml -o ~/.config/i3/config

Send us themes!

If you have a colorscheme you'd like to share, you can convert an existing i3 config to a theme file:

# Show the next scratchpad window or hide the focused scratchpad window.
# If there are multiple scratchpad windows, this command cycles through them.
bindsym Mod1+minus scratchpad show

# switch to workspace
bindsym Mod1+1 workspace 1
bindsym Mod1+2 workspace 2
bindsym Mod1+3 workspace 3
bindsym Mod1+4 workspace 4
bindsym Mod1+5 workspace 5
bindsym Mod1+6 workspace 6
bindsym Mod1+7 workspace 7
bindsym Mod1+8 workspace 8
bindsym Mod1+9 workspace 9
bindsym Mod1+0 workspace 10

# move focused container to workspace
bindsym Mod1+Shift+1 move container to workspace 1
bindsym Mod1+Shift+2 move container to workspace 2
bindsym Mod1+Shift+3 move container to workspace 3
bindsym Mod1+Shift+4 move container to workspace 4
bindsym Mod1+Shift+5 move container to workspace 5
bindsym Mod1+Shift+6 move container to workspace 6
bindsym Mod1+Shift+7 move container to workspace 7
bindsym Mod1+Shift+8 move container to workspace 8
bindsym Mod1+Shift+9 move container to workspace 9
bindsym Mod1+Shift+0 move container to workspace 10

# reload the configuration file
bindsym Mod1+Shift+c reload
# restart i3 inplace (preserves your layout/session, can be used to upgrade i3)
bindsym Mod1+Shift+r restart
# exit i3 (logs you out of your X session)
bindsym Mod1+Shift+e exec "i3-nagbar -t warning -m 'You pressed the exit shortcut. Do you really want to exit i3? This will end your X session.' -b 'Yes, exit i3' 'i3-msg exit'"

# resize window (you can also use the mouse for that)
mode "resize" {
        # These bindings trigger as soon as you enter the resize mode

        # Pressing left will shrink the window’s width.
        # Pressing right will grow the window’s width.
        # Pressing up will shrink the window’s height.
        # Pressing down will grow the window’s height.
        bindsym j           resize shrink width 10 px or 10 ppt
        bindsym k           resize grow height 10 px or 10 ppt
        bindsym l           resize shrink height 10 px or 10 ppt
        bindsym semicolon   resize grow width 10 px or 10 ppt

        # same bindings, but for the arrow keys
        bindsym Left        resize shrink width 10 px or 10 ppt
        bindsym Down        resize grow height 10 px or 10 ppt
        bindsym Up          resize shrink height 10 px or 10 ppt
        bindsym Right       resize grow width 10 px or 10 ppt

        # back to normal: Enter or Escape
        bindsym Return mode "default"
        bindsym Escape mode "default"
}

bindsym Mod1+r mode "resize"

# Start i3bar to display a workspace bar (plus the system information i3status
# finds out, if available)

        status_command i3status
  colors {
    separator #AAAAAA
    background #222133
    statusline #FFFFFF

    active_workspace #DCCD69 #DCCD69 #181715

import subprocess, os, re, sys
env = dict(os.environ); env['PATH'] = '/tmp/fakebin:' + env['PATH']
def name_batch(cols):
    # cols: up to 28 hex strings (with #)

    c = list(cols) + [cols[-1]]*(28-len(cols))
    lines = []
    lines.append("bar {\n colors {")
    lines.append(f"  separator {c[0]}")
    lines.append(f"  background {c[1]}")
    lines.append(f"  statusline {c[2]}")
    lines.append(f"  focused_workspace {c[3]} {c[4]} {c[5]}")
    lines.append(f"  inactive_workspace {c[6]} {c[7]} {c[8]}")
    lines.append(f"  urgent_workspace {c[9]} {c[10]} {c[11]}")
    lines.append(" }\n}")
    i = 12

        lines.append(f"client.{k} {c[i]} {c[i+1]} {c[i+2]} {c[i+3]}"); i += 4
    open('/tmp/h/nb.conf','w').write("\n".join(lines)+"\n")

    m = {}

    for line in sec.splitlines():
        mm = re.match(r'^  (\S+): "(#[0-9A-F]+)"$', line)
        if mm: m[mm.group(2)] = re.sub(r'-\d+$','',mm.group(1))
    return {col: m[col.upper()] for col in cols}
def name_all(cols):
    res = {}

    for i in range(0, len(cols), 28):
        res.update(name_batch(cols[i:i+28]))
    return res
if __name__ == '__main__':
    print(name_all(sys.argv[1:]))

import json, sys, math, random
r=json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
A,B=sys.argv[2],sys.argv[3]
c=[int(sys.argv[4][i:i+2],16) for i in (0,2,4)]
pts=[]
for h,n in r.items():
    p=[int(h[i:i+2],16)-c[k] for k,i in enumerate((1,3,5))]
    if n==A: pts.append((p,1))
    elif n==B: pts.append((p,-1))
# model: A wins iff w.p > t ; search over sphere
best=None
N=400
for i in range(N):
  th=math.acos(1-2*(i+0.5)/N)
  for j in range(N):
    ph=2*math.pi*j/N
    w=(math.sin(th)*math.cos(ph), math.sin(th)*math.sin(ph), math.cos(th))
    vals=sorted((sum(a*b for a,b in zip(w,p)),s) for p,s in pts)
    # best threshold
    # count errors for threshold between vals
    tot_pos=sum(1 for v,s in vals if s==1)
    err=tot_pos  # threshold below all: all predicted A(+1) -> errors = negatives count
    err=sum(1 for v,s in vals if s==-1)
    bestt=(err, vals[0][0]-1)
    for k,(v,s) in enumerate(vals):
        if s==-1: err-=1
        else: err+=1
        if err<bestt[0]: bestt=(err, v+1e-9)
    if best is None or bestt[0]<best[0]: best=(bestt[0], w, bestt[1])
print(best, len(pts))

def redmean(p, q):
    rm=(p[0]+q[0])/2
    dr,dg,db=p[0]-q[0],p[1]-q[1],p[2]-q[2]
    return (2+rm/256)*dr*dr+4*dg*dg+(2+(255-rm)/256)*db*db
def de76(p,q):
    a,b=lab(p),lab(q); return sum((x-y)**2 for x,y in zip(a,b))
def de94(p,q):
    L1,a1,b1=lab(p); L2,a2,b2=lab(q)
    dL=L1-L2; C1=(a1*a1+b1*b1)**.5; C2=(a2*a2+b2*b2)**.5; dC=C1-C2
    da=a1-a2; db=b1-b2; dH2=max(da*da+db*db-dC*dC,0)
    SL=1; SC=1+0.045*C1; SH=1+0.015*C1
    return (dL/SL)**2+(dC/SC)**2+dH2/SH**2
def de2000(p,q):
    import math
    L1,a1,b1=lab(p); L2,a2,b2=lab(q)
    C1=math.hypot(a1,b1); C2=math.hypot(a2,b2); Cb=(C1+C2)/2
    G=0.5*(1-math.sqrt(Cb**7/(Cb**7+25**7)))
    a1p=(1+G)*a1; a2p=(1+G)*a2
    C1p=math.hypot(a1p,b1); C2p=math.hypot(a2p,b2)
    h1p=math.degrees(math.atan2(b1,a1p))%360; h2p=math.degrees(math.atan2(b2,a2p))%360
    dLp=L2-L1; dCp=C2p-C1p
    dhp=h2p-h1p
    if C1p*C2p==0: dhp=0
    elif dhp>180: dhp-=360
    elif dhp<-180: dhp+=360
    dHp=2*math.sqrt(C1p*C2p)*math.sin(math.radians(dhp/2))
    Lbp=(L1+L2)/2; Cbp=(C1p+C2p)/2
    if C1p*C2p==0: hbp=h1p+h2p

import subprocess, os, re, json
env = dict(os.environ); env['PATH'] = '/tmp/fakebin:' + env['PATH']
def run(theme, conf):
    open('/tmp/h/ex.conf','w').write(conf)
    r = subprocess.run(['/workspace/executable',theme,'-c','/tmp/h/ex.conf'],capture_output=True,text=True,env=env)
    return r.stdout, r.stderr, r.returncode
lst = subprocess.run(['/workspace/executable','-l'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout
themes = []
for line in lst.splitlines():
    m = re.match(r'^  (\S+)\s+- (.*)$', line)
    if m: themes.append((m.group(1), m.group(2)))
classes = ['focused','focused_inactive','unfocused','urgent']
ws = ['focused_workspace','active_workspace','inactive_workspace','urgent_workspace']
simple = ['separator','background','statusline']
conf = ""
for i,c in enumerate(classes):
    conf += f"client.{c}  O{i}a O{i}b O{i}c O{i}d EXTRA\n"
conf += "bar {\n  colors {\n"
for i,s in enumerate(simple): conf += f"    {s} S{i}\n"
for i,w in enumerate(ws): conf += f"    {w}  W{i}a W{i}b W{i}c\n"
conf += "  }\n}\n"
out = {}
for name, desc in themes:
    o,e,rc = run(name, conf)
    assert rc == 0, (name, e)
    t = {'description': desc}
    lines = o.splitlines()
    wc = {}
    for i,c in enumerate(classes):
        l = lines[i]
        if l == f"client.{c}  O{i}a O{i}b O{i}c O{i}d EXTRA":
            wc[c] = None
        else:
            toks = l.split(' ')
            assert toks[0] == f"client.{c}", l
            vals = toks[1:5]
            olds = [f"O{i}a", f"O{i}b", f"O{i}c", f"O{i}d"]
            wc[c] = {k: (None if v == ov else v) for k, v, ov in zip(['border','background','text','indicator'], vals, olds)}
    t['window_colors'] = wc
    bc = {}
    for i,s in enumerate(simple):
        l = lines[6+i]
        v = l.split(' ')[-1]
        bc[s] = None if v == f"S{i}" else v
    for i,w in enumerate(ws):
        l = lines[9+i]
        if l == f"    {w}  W{i}a W{i}b W{i}c":
            bc[w] = None
        else:
            toks = l.strip().split(' ')
            olds = [f"W{i}a", f"W{i}b", f"W{i}c"]
            bc[w] = {k: (None if v == ov else v) for k, v, ov in zip(['border','background','text'], toks[1:4], olds)}
    t['bar_colors'] = bc
    # check None-ness of window_colors / bar_colors
    o2,e2,rc2 = run(name, "x\n")
    t['wc_none'] = 'writer.rs:435:59' in e2
    t['tail_noclients'] = o2
    o3,e3,rc3 = run(name, "bar {\n  colors {\n  }\n}\n")
    t['bc_none'] = 'writer.rs:59:61' in e3
    t['bar_append'] = o3
    out[name] = t
json.dump(out, open('/tmp/h/themes.json','w'), indent=1)
for k,v in out.items(): print(k, v['wc_none'], v['bc_none'], [c for c in classes if v['window_colors'][c] is None], [w for w in ws+simple if v['bar_colors'][w] is None])
EOF

**How I checked it:** I ran both binaries side by side, with a fake `i3`/`i3-msg` on the PATH, over several thousand cases. These included fixed test suites, random command lines, random configs and themes, mutated YAML files, the bundled default i3 config, and a realistic config using `$variables`. The default config with the `purple` theme reproduces `assets/default-config-purple.expected` exactly.

**What it covers:**
- **Applying a theme:** built-in themes or a YAML file, written to stdout or via `-o`/`-s` (through the `i3-style/<n>/` temp directory), plus `-r`. It keeps the original's quirks, such as:
  - lines split only on spaces;
  - unknown entries inside a bar's `colors` block are dropped;
  - missing entries are added with doubled indentation and a trailing space;
  - missing `client.*` lines are added with `#000000` defaults;
  - a stray 4th token is kept on workspace lines.
- **Built-in themes:** all 19 are included. I recovered their colour values by applying each one to test configs; `flat-gray` correctly has a few entries missing.
- **Theme files:** parsed by a YAML reader written to behave like the yaml-rust library the original uses. Its parse-error messages and positions matched on every invalid input I tried.
- **`--to-theme`:** produces the same YAML, including which bar entries are left out and the colour-naming order.
- **Colour names:** the nearest of 140 HTML colours, by plain RGB distance. Ties are broken by the original in a way I couldn't explain, so I measured its answer for all 16.7 million colours and store the tie results in a 76 KB file, `src/tie_runs.bin`. With that table my namer matches the original on every colour.
- **Command line:** copies the old clap 2 behaviour, including usage lines, the coloured "Did you mean" hints, red/yellow/green errors when stderr is a terminal, and the default value for `-t`.
- **Crash messages:** the original's Rust-style panic messages are reproduced word for word, including the source locations it reports (which line kind was being written when a pipe closed, invalid UTF-8, bad hex colours, and so on).

**Where it may still differ:**
- If several argument errors happen at once (for example a flag given twice and a missing value), the original reports one at random on each run; mine always picks the same one.
- When looking for a default config I only check `~/.i3/config` and `~/.config/i3/config`. I couldn't test whether the original also looks in `/etc`, because I have no root access to create files there.
- With `RUST_BACKTRACE` set, the original prints a backtrace after a crash; mine does not.

During the work I moved the original binary to `/tmp/orig_executable` so `compile.sh` could write `./executable` in its place.

**What it is:** a Rust program with no external crates (about 4,500 lines in `src/`). `compile.sh` runs `cargo build --release --offline` and copies the result to `./executable`; it falls back to plain `rustc` if cargo is missing. A fresh clone builds with it. `/target` and `/executable` are in `.gitignore`.

**What it covers:**
- **Command line:** the original was built with clap 2.34, so I copied its behaviour: help and version text, every error message, "Did you mean" suggestions, the usage line in errors, colours when stderr is a terminal, and non-UTF-8 arguments.
- **Applying a theme:** the line-by-line rewriting of an i3 config, including the original's quirks: tab-separated lines aren't recognised, an extra old token is kept on workspace lines, and appended or inserted lines have specific indentation and trailing spaces. A rebuilt i3 default config with the `purple` theme produces exactly `assets/default-config-purple.expected`.
- **Theme files:** a YAML reader that behaves like the yaml-rust library the original uses, down to its exact parse-error messages and positions.
- **`--to-theme`:** builds the YAML output and names each colour after the nearest HTML colour.
- **Other flows:** finding the config in `~/.i3/config` or `~/.config/i3/config`, checking it with `i3 -C`, the `-o`/`-s` temporary-copy flow, and `-r` (`i3-msg reload`).
- **Crash output:** where the original crashes (missing files, short config lines, invalid YAML or hex), it prints a Rust panic naming a source line and exits 101. I reproduce the same text and exit code.

**One part is a data table, not a formula.** Colour naming is nearest-colour by plain RGB distance, but when two names are equally close the original's choice follows no rule I could find. I queried the original for all 16.7 million colours and stored its tie-break choices in `src/tie_runs.bin` (76 KB). My implementation now names every colour the same as the original.

**Testing:** I ran thousands of side-by-side comparisons against the original: fixed cases, plus randomised configs, themes, YAML and argument combinations.

**Known differences:**
- When several argument errors occur at once (e.g. `-lr -lr`), the original picks which to report at random from run to run, so neither version is predictable there.
- When `HOME` has no config, I only search `~/.i3/config` and `~/.config/i3/config`. I couldn't test whether the original also checks `/etc/i3/config` (I couldn't create files there), so if it does, mine won't.
- The `-o` temporary folder name is time-based (seconds plus milliseconds), so it differs from run to run in both versions.

Testing needs a stand-in `i3` command on the PATH, because i3 isn't installed here and both versions refuse to apply a theme without it. To build mine in place I moved the original binary to `/tmp/orig_executable`; `./executable` in the workspace is now my build.
